(CNN) -- The bodies of young elephants covered in the brown dirt of dried-up wells tell a heartrending story. A baby elephant in the Gourma region of central Mali had been trapped in a well for three days. Reaching desperately for drops of water, they had lowered their trunks, toppled in, remained trapped and died in Mali's scorching heat. The "last desert elephants in West Africa" have "adapted to survive in the harsh conditions" they face, Save the Elephants said Monday. But now, the group says, conditions have gone from bad to worse, and they are living "on the margin of what is ecologically viable." Save the Elephants distributed new pictures Monday that depict the devastating drought and the struggle for survival in Mali, one of the poorest nations in the world. "Six elephants have already been found dead," the group wrote in a news release accompanying the photos. "Four others, including three calves, were recently extracted from a shallow well into which they had fallen when searching for water. Only the largest survived." The youngest are in the most danger, since their smaller trunks can't reach deep into the few remaining wells, the group said. The worst drought in 26 years is threatening the existence of the "last desert elephants in West Africa," the northernmost herds in the continent, Save the Elephants said. The animals, now numbering only about 350 to 450, have been called "the last elephants of Timbuktu," said Jake Wall, a scientist with Save the Elephants. But they're south of Timbuktu, Wall told CNN in a phone interview from Bamako, Mali. "We tend to refer to them as 'the last Sahelian elephants.' "  See a map of Mali » . Each year, the elephants trek farther on the fringes of the Sahara to find water. They have the longest migration route of any in the continent, traveling "in a counterclockwise circle" of about 700 kilometers (435 miles), Save the Elephants said. The images are signs of the crisis gripping the northwest African nation. The U.N. Development Programme ranks Mali near the bottom of its Human Development Index. It cites a 56 percent poverty rate in the country, with nearly a third of the population unlikely to live past age 40, and an illiteracy rate of 77 percent. The World Food Programme says the majority of infant deaths in Mali are due to malnutrition. The drought, combined with soaring temperatures, has also led to deaths of cattle, Save the Elephants said. "The stench of rotting corpses fills the air, and what little water remains is putrid and undrinkable by all standards." In areas where the elephants live and search for water, "the normal peaceful coexistence between the elephants and herdsmen is starting to break down and giving way to conflict over access to water," Wall said. There is some hope for the weeks and months ahead. "We're hoping the rains start in June, and that will allow the elephants to start drinking out of shallow ponds until the really heavy rains begin" in July or August, Wall said. But "urgent action" is needed in the interim "to secure water for the elephants," Wall's group said in its news release. Save the Elephants, which focuses on helping elephant populations worldwide, said it has partnered with a foundation and the Mali government in its fundraising appeal.

(CNN) -- The bodies of young elephants, coated in the brown dust of dried-up wells, tell a heartrending story. In the Gourma region of central Mali, a baby elephant had been trapped in a well for three days. Reaching desperately for drops of water, these animals had lowered their trunks, lost their footing, and tumbled in—becoming trapped and ultimately perishing in Mali's scorching heat.

The "last desert elephants in West Africa" have long "adapted to survive in the harsh conditions" they face, Save the Elephants reported Monday. But now, the organization warns, conditions have deteriorated from bad to worse, leaving these animals to survive "on the margin of what is ecologically viable."

Save the Elephants released new photographs Monday depicting the devastating drought and the elephants' struggle for survival in Mali, one of the world's poorest nations. "Six elephants have already been found dead," the group stated in a news release accompanying the images. "Four others, including three calves, were recently extracted from a shallow well into which they had fallen while searching for water. Only the largest survived."

The youngest elephants face the greatest peril, as their smaller trunks cannot reach the depths of the few remaining wells, according to the group.

This drought—the worst in 26 years—threatens the very existence of the "last desert elephants in West Africa," the northernmost herds on the continent, Save the Elephants said. Numbering only about 350 to 450 individuals, these animals have been dubbed "the last elephants of Timbuktu," according to Jake Wall, a scientist with the organization. However, Wall clarified in a phone interview with CNN from Bamako, Mali, that the herds actually range south of Timbuktu. "We tend to refer to them as 'the last Sahelian elephants,'" he explained.

*See a map of Mali »*

Each year, these elephants journey farther into the fringes of the Sahara in search of water, undertaking the longest migration route of any elephant population on the continent—a counterclockwise circuit spanning roughly 700 kilometers (435 miles), according to Save the Elephants.

These haunting images reflect the broader crisis gripping this northwest African nation. The U.N. Development Programme ranks Mali near the bottom of its Human Development Index, citing a 56 percent poverty rate, a life expectancy below 40 for nearly a third of the population, and a 77 percent illiteracy rate. The World Food Programme reports that malnutrition accounts for the majority of infant deaths in the country.

The drought, compounded by soaring temperatures, has also claimed the lives of cattle, Save the Elephants noted. "The stench of rotting corpses fills the air, and what little water remains is putrid and undrinkable by all standards."

# The Last Sahelian Elephants Face a Deadly Reckoning

In the arid expanse of Mali's Gourma region, a heartbreaking crisis is unfolding as young elephants meet tragic ends while searching for one of life's most basic necessities: water. Desperate calves, driven by thirst in an increasingly parched landscape, have been falling into dried-up wells—remnants of once-reliable water sources now transformed into deadly traps. Some of these young animals have remained stuck for agonizing days, exposed to relentless heat, before ultimately succumbing to exhaustion and dehydration.

## Living on the Edge of Survival

According to Save the Elephants, an organization dedicated to monitoring and protecting these magnificent creatures, the desert elephants of West Africa represent a remarkable example of adaptation to extreme environments. These animals have historically demonstrated extraordinary resilience, developing behaviors and physiological traits that allow them to thrive where few large mammals could survive. However, the organization warns that worsening drought conditions have pushed this population to what they describe as "the margin of ecological viability"—a precarious threshold where the very adaptations that once ensured their survival may no longer be sufficient to sustain them.

## A Mounting Death Toll

The severity of the current crisis has become increasingly apparent through devastating statistics. Six elephants have already been confirmed dead, victims of the deepening water shortage. In a particularly harrowing incident, four elephants—including three young calves—were discovered trapped in a shallow well and required rescue efforts to free them. Tragically, only the largest of these four animals survived the ordeal, highlighting the vulnerability of the youngest members of this elephant population.

## Why Young Elephants Are Most at Risk

The disproportionate impact on calves stems from a critical physical limitation: their smaller trunks simply cannot reach the deep water that remains in the few wells still containing any moisture. As drought conditions have intensified and water tables have dropped, adult elephants—with their longer trunks—retain the ability to access these deeper water sources. Young elephants, however, are left dangerously exposed, forced into increasingly risky situations as they attempt to quench their thirst, sometimes with fatal consequences.

## A Population Under Unprecedented Threat

This drought represents the most severe conditions the region has experienced in 26 years, placing extraordinary pressure on a population that was already vulnerable due to its small size. Numbering somewhere between 350 and 450 individuals, these animals are known as "the last Sahelian elephants"—a designation that underscores both their ecological significance and their precarious status as survivors of a once more widespread population.

What makes this population particularly remarkable is their extraordinary migratory behavior. Each year, these elephants undertake the longest migration route of any elephant population in Africa, traveling in a vast counterclockwise circle spanning roughly 700 kilometers. This epic journey, likely developed over generations as an adaptation to the challenging Sahelian environment, now faces disruption as traditional water sources dry up and the delicate balance that has sustained this migration pattern is thrown into jeopardy.

The current crisis serves as a stark reminder of how climate change and worsening drought conditions can push even remarkably adapted species to the brink, threatening not just individual animals but the survival of an entire unique population that has called this challenging landscape home for generations.

The Gourma has historically been home to nomadic and semi-nomadic populations, including Fulani, Tuareg, and Dogon communities, who have relied on traditional livestock herding and seasonal migration patterns. # Mali's Desert Elephants: A Species on the Brink Amid Devastating Drought

**GOURMA REGION, Mali** — For centuries, they carved invisible paths through some of the harshest terrain on Earth, following ancient migratory routes across the Sahel in search of water. Now, conservationists warn that Mali's iconic desert elephants — among the most resilient megafauna on the planet — are dying at an alarming rate as an unprecedented drought grips the region.

The Gourma elephants, known for undertaking the longest land migration of any elephant population in the world, have long been considered a symbol of extraordinary adaptation. But wildlife officials and environmental groups say the current dry spell, compounded by years of below-average rainfall, is pushing the population past its breaking point.

"We are witnessing something we feared but hoped we would never see," said a spokesperson for the Mali Elephant Project, one of the organizations that has tracked the herd for more than two decades. "These are animals that have survived droughts before. But this one is different in scale and duration."

## A Population Already Fragile

Numbering in the low hundreds even in stable years, the Gourma elephants represent one of the last populations of desert-adapted elephants in West Africa. Unlike elephants in more temperate regions, this herd has evolved behaviors suited to extreme scarcity — traveling vast distances between watering holes, sometimes over 30 miles in a single trek, and timing migrations with a precision passed down through generations.

Conservationists say that precision is now being upended. Watering holes the elephants have relied on for generations have dried up entirely. Vegetation that once provided crucial nutrition during dry months has failed to regenerate. Satellite tracking collars placed on several elephants show erratic movement patterns, with animals wandering farther from traditional routes in what researchers believe is a desperate search for water.

## Compounding Crises

The drought is not occurring in isolation. Mali's elephants already faced mounting pressures from armed conflict in the region, which has restricted access for conservation patrols and made it more difficult to monitor herd health or intervene during crises. Climate change has intensified rainfall variability across the Sahel, while human populations competing for the same dwindling water resources have added further strain on the delicate ecological balance the elephants depend upon.

"This is a perfect storm," said one regional environmental official who requested anonymity due to security concerns. "You have climate stress, conflict limiting our ability to respond, and a population that was already vulnerable before this drought began."

Local carcass counts, though difficult to verify precisely given ongoing instability in the region, suggest a mortality rate that conservationists describe as catastrophic relative to the population's small size. Several calves are reported among the dead, raising fears about the herd's ability to recover even if conditions improve.

## What Comes Next

International conservation groups are scrambling to mobilize emergency water delivery efforts, though logistics remain complicated by both the remoteness of the terrain and ongoing security concerns in the region. Some experts have called for emergency intervention, including artificial water points, though such measures are complicated by cost, logistics, and the risk of altering natural migratory behavior long-term.

Others say the moment demands a broader reckoning.

"This isn't just about one herd of elephants," said a wildlife biologist who has studied the population for years. "It's a signal of what's happening across the Sahel, and a warning about what unchecked climate change and habitat pressure can do to species that took thousands of years to adapt to their environment."

For now, researchers continue monitoring what remains of the herd, documenting losses in real time while racing to determine whether meaningful intervention is still possible — or whether Mali's desert elephants, after generations of extraordinary endurance, are witnessing their final chapter.

*This story reflects the ongoing and evolving situation in the Gourma region. Details continue to be assessed by wildlife organizations and local authorities.*

Their annual migration circuit, covering distances of up to 12,000 km, was documented extensively through satellite tracking collaborations between Malian conservation authorities and international partners, including Save the Elephants (STE).

# Young Elephants Perish in Wells as Historic Drought Grips Mali

**GOURMA REGION, Mali** — Wildlife conservationists are reporting a distressing pattern of deaths among Mali's endangered desert elephants, as prolonged drought conditions have driven young elephants into man-made wells in search of water, often with fatal consequences.

The Gourma elephants, one of the last remaining populations of desert-adapted elephants in West Africa, undertake one of the longest land migrations of any elephant population, traveling in a roughly 32,000-square-kilometer loop across Mali in search of seasonal water and vegetation. This year's drought has reportedly been more severe and prolonged than in recent memory, shrinking natural waterholes and forcing herds to rely increasingly on deep wells dug by local communities.

## A Deadly Search for Water

According to conservationists monitoring the herds, calves and juvenile elephants—less experienced and physically weaker than adults—have become trapped or fallen into these wells while attempting to reach water at the bottom. Several have died from exhaustion, injury, or inability to escape before rescuers or family members could intervene.

"When surface water disappears, elephants are forced to dig or use existing wells, and this is where young ones are most vulnerable," said one regional wildlife biologist familiar with the population. "Their mothers and herd members will try to help pull them out, but the wells are often too deep or narrow, and by the time local herders or conservation teams arrive, it can be too late."

## Compounding Pressures

Experts note that this crisis reflects broader challenges facing the Gourma elephants, whose population has already been reduced by poaching, habitat loss, and competition with livestock for dwindling resources. Climate variability in the Sahel has made rainfall increasingly unpredictable, shortening the window during which natural water sources remain available.

"This population has survived one of the harshest environments any elephant faces on Earth," said a conservation officer with a regional wildlife protection group. "But repeated severe droughts, on top of existing pressures, could tip things toward serious long-term decline if mitigation efforts aren't scaled up."

## Community and Conservation Response

# Last Elephants of Timbuktu Face Fight for Survival as Water Sources Vanish

In the arid landscapes surrounding Mali's legendary desert city, one of Africa's most remarkable wildlife populations is teetering on the edge of extinction. The Mali elephants—famous for undertaking the longest land migration of any elephant population on Earth—are running out of water, and with it, time.

## A Migration Like No Other

For generations, these elephants have traversed roughly 300 miles annually across the Gourma region near Timbuktu, following an ancient circular route between seasonal water holes and grazing lands. This extraordinary journey, unmatched by any other elephant population in the world, has allowed the species to survive in one of the harshest environments elephants are known to inhabit.

But conservationists now warn that the delicate balance sustaining this migration has been shattered.

## Conservation Groups Sound the Alarm

According to field researchers and conservation organizations monitoring the population, including groups such as the Mali Elephant Project, prolonged drought conditions—worsened by climate change—have caused critical water points along the elephants' traditional route to dry up earlier and more severely than in past years.

"We're seeing water sources that elephants have relied on for decades simply disappearing," conservationists tracking the herds have reported. "When the watering holes fail, the entire migratory pattern that has sustained this population begins to break down."

The consequences have been dire. Reports from the region describe elephants traveling far outside their normal range in search of water, increasing deadly encounters with local communities who are themselves struggling with the same resource scarcity. Competition between humans and elephants for dwindling water and grazing land has intensified tensions in an area already strained by insecurity.

## A Population Already Vulnerable

Numbering only a few hundred individuals, the Mali elephants represent one of the most fragile populations on the continent. Unlike elephant herds in East or Southern Africa that number in the tens of thousands, this isolated population has almost no margin for error.

Conservationists note that the elephants face a convergence of threats: prolonged drought, habitat degradation, and ongoing regional conflict that has made monitoring and protection efforts increasingly dangerous for rangers and researchers alike. Armed conflict in the region has periodically forced conservation teams to suspend operations, leaving the elephants more vulnerable during critical dry periods.

## Climate Change as the Underlying Threat

Experts point to shifting rainfall patterns as the root cause of the crisis. The Sahel region, where Timbuktu is located, has experienced increasingly erratic and diminished rainfall over the past several decades. For elephants that depend on predictable seasonal water cycles, even minor disruptions can prove catastrophic.

"This isn't just a local water shortage—it's a symptom of a much larger climate crisis reshaping the Sahel," conservation researchers have emphasized. "These elephants are essentially climate refugees, and they have nowhere left to go."

## What's Being Done

Conservation groups have called for urgent international support to fund emergency water interventions, including the drilling of boreholes and creation of artificial water points along the elephants' migratory corridor. Community engagement programs aimed at reducing human-elephant conflict have also been proposed as essential to the population's survival.

However, funding remains a persistent challenge, compounded by the security risks associated with operating in the region.

## A Race Against Time

For now, the fate of the Timbuktu elephants hangs in a precarious balance. Conservationists warn that without immediate and sustained intervention, this population—along with the ancient migratory tradition it represents—could vanish within a generation.

As one conservationist put it: "These elephants have survived droughts before. But what they're facing now is different. The question isn't just whether they can adapt—it's whether we'll give them the chance to."
